name: Miller's Law
description: Human working memory reliably holds around 7 (plus or minus 2) discrete chunks of information at once.
design_relevance_note: Often cited to justify limiting navigation menu items or choices — worth citing carefully given the figure itself has been contested.
myth_risk_note: The simplified 'magic number seven' claim vastly oversimplifies working memory capacity, which is demonstrably more flexible and context-dependent than the named law suggests, despite confirmed existence of capacity limits.
prevalence_note: The '7±2' figure is extremely widely cited in UX writing on menu/option-count design, despite being one of the most commonly misapplied laws in this taxonomy.

findings.description: Human short-term/working memory reliably holds approximately 7 (plus or minus 2) discrete chunks of information at once — a foundational estimate of working-memory capacity, though the specific figure has since been contested and refined by later research.
findings.source_title: The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information

applications.title: Hypothetical: designers who cap navigation menus at 7 items, misapplying Miller's 'magic number'
applications.description: NN/g describes a common, genuine misapplication of Miller's 1956 finding: designers refusing to add more than seven items to a global navigation menu out of fear of violating the 'magical number seven,' even though Miller's finding concerns short-term memory recall, not on-screen recognition -- menus rely on recognition (all options stay visible), so there is no usability cost to exceeding seven well-structured items.
applications.ethical_note: This is a myth-busting entry about misapplying a real, well-established memory-research finding to an unrelated design context (recognition-based menus, not recall-based memory tasks) -- directly aligned with this corpus's own purpose of separating genuine science from popular misuse, with no persuasion or user-manipulation dimension involved.
